blocks.content: A Compose file has a small, predictable shape: a top-level services block (required), and optional top-level networks and volumes blocks for anything shared across services.

Almost every Compose file is built from the same three top-level sections: services (the containers themselves, required), networks (any custom networks beyond the automatic default), and volumes (any named volumes services need to reference).

blocks.alt: Three top-level sections cover almost every Compose file

blocks.content:
services:
  # ... one block per container ...
networks:
  # ... optional, custom networks ...
volumes:
  # ... optional, named volumes ...

code.content:
services:
  # ... one block per container ...
networks:
  # ... optional, custom networks ...
volumes:
  # ... optional, named volumes ...

codes.yaml:
services:
  # ... one block per container ...
networks:
  # ... optional, custom networks ...
volumes:
  # ... optional, named volumes ...

blocks.content: Inside services, each named block describes one container: either image (pull an existing image) or build (build one from a local Dockerfile), plus whatever ports, environment variables, and volumes that specific service needs.

blocks.alt: Each service block mirrors a single docker run command

blocks.content: A named volume meant to be used by one or more services is declared once, at the top level, under volumes, then referenced by name from within any service that needs it, covered in full in the dedicated Volumes topic later in this module.

blocks.alt: Declared once, referenced by name wherever needed

blocks.content: Put together, a realistic Compose file reads naturally once you know the shape: a handful of named services, each with its own configuration, plus whatever shared networks and volumes tie them together.

blocks.alt: The complete shape, once every piece is in place

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A Compose file is built from three top-level sections: services (required), and optional networks and volumes for anything shared.
Each entry under services mirrors what would otherwise be a separate docker run command, with its own image/build, ports, and environment.
